threads.thread_goal: Align on current procedures and confirm scope of the integrated support programme.

messages.text: Morning all. To get the Integrated Early Support Programme for At-Risk Children moving, could we share how we currently identify and refer children we are worried about? The aim is to pull this into the Current Procedures Mapping Document for the pilot. That will sit in project_pack_ref: Integrated Early Support Programme for At-Risk Children as A1 and link to task T1. It will also feed into the Pilot Plan and Schedule (A7) and task T9 on the pilot scope. Please describe briefly: 1) what you notice first, 2) who you talk to, 3) what form or system you use, 4) how social services get involved.

From my side in class: 1) First signs are usually changes in mood, withdrawal, frequent crying, or sudden aggression, plus repeated tiredness or missed days. 2) I speak with the class teacher and sometimes the school nurse if it looks health related. 3) We log concerns in the school incident / concern form and in the class notes, but it is not very standardised. 4) Social services are usually contacted by the school leader after a meeting with parents, unless there is an urgent safeguarding concern where leadership calls directly. This is not written as a clear flow yet, so A1 from T1 will really help.

In my group it is similar but maybe a bit more informal. I notice things like a child not joining play, clinging to adults, or big changes in toileting or eating. I usually talk first with the teacher and sometimes with the previous key worker if the child is new. We write notes in the child observation book and sometimes in the digital system, but I am not sure we always flag it in the same way. For social services, I have mostly seen leadership handle the contact. I can help describe these steps for A1 under T1, but I might need someone to check I captured the social work side correctly.

From the community social work side: 1) We receive referrals mainly from school leadership, health visitors, or directly from parents. 2) First contact is usually a phone call or secure email from school, followed by our intake triage. 3) We log the case in the social services system and open an initial assessment. 4) For safeguarding, we follow the organisational guidelines strictly and may visit the home quickly. I can take the lead on mapping the social work steps for A1 under T1, including where consent and data protection checks happen, and then share a draft for you to confirm.

Adding from my classroom: we often spot patterns like repeated minor injuries, very inconsistent attendance, or children who seem very anxious at separation. I raise it in our weekly class check-in with the teacher. We use the same incident / concern form as 499701 mentioned, but I also keep a simple tally of incidents to see trends. I think this could be standardised into A1 so that when we move to the Pilot Plan and Schedule (A7) and T9, we know exactly which concerns should trigger the new protocol.

Thanks all, this is helpful. To move T1 forward, I can start a simple table for A1 with columns for: trigger signs, school steps, forms / systems, and social work steps. 361403, could you add the detailed social work flow, especially where consent is needed and when we bypass parents due to safeguarding? Then 499701 and 511446 can check the school side. Once A1 is stable, we can use it to shape A7 and T9 for the pilot scope.

Yes, I can add the social work flow into A1 today under T1. I will include: intake triage, risk rating, consent checks, and when we escalate to safeguarding procedures. I will also note which cases we currently decline or redirect, as that will matter for T9 when we define which types of cases are in scope for the pilot.

Once you have the first version of A1, please share the link. I can review the school steps for T1 and add examples from two classes, including how we currently handle children with learning difficulties versus mainly social-emotional concerns. That should help us later when we decide which types of cases to include in the pilot under T9.

I can also check A1 from the point of view of workload in the classroom. For example, some of the current steps are quite time consuming during busy times. If we capture that clearly in T1, we can design the pilot in A7 and T9 so that new routines fit into the day without overloading staff.

I will look at A1 as well and add notes on how we currently involve parents when we first raise concerns, especially for younger children. It might not be as structured as it could be, but at least we will have a baseline for T1 before we design the new family engagement pieces later.

On the pilot scope for T9 and A7: based on capacity, I suggest we start with two classes in the same year group, focusing on children where there are repeated wellbeing or safety concerns but not active child protection investigations. That way we respect safeguarding rules and can still test the new joint protocol. Does that feel realistic from the school side?

Two classes sounds manageable to me, especially if we keep the focus on early concerns rather than the most complex protection cases. I would propose we include both behaviour / learning concerns and social-emotional worries, as long as we are clear in A7 and T9 that we are not replacing existing safeguarding procedures. We should also check with school leadership before we confirm.

Agree with two classes. I would also suggest we cap the number of active children per class in the pilot, maybe around five per class, so that we can realistically follow the new routines. We can note that assumption in A7 and T9 and adjust later if needed.

From my view, two classes and focusing on early concerns rather than open protection cases feels safer and more realistic. I will draft a short pilot scope section in A7 under T9 with: two classes in the same year group, up to five children per class, and excluding children already in formal child protection processes. I will then ask school leadership to confirm.

To summarise and check we are aligned before I update A7 and T9: we are proposing that the pilot covers two classes in the same year group, with up to five at-risk children per class, focusing on early wellbeing, learning, and safety concerns, and not including children already in formal child protection investigations. If no one objects by tomorrow, I will treat this as our agreed pilot scope and note it as such in A7.

No objections from me. That scope feels workable in the classroom and should give us enough variety of cases to test the new protocol. Once A1 is complete under T1, we can double check that the types of concerns we see most often are covered within this scope.

On ownership for the Current Procedures Mapping Document (A1, T1): 361403 will lead on the social work sections, and I can coordinate the school side and pull everything into one document. 499701, 511446, and 350111 will review and add classroom details. I will also make sure one community social worker and one early years assistant review the final version, as required in T1.

Confirmed from my side: I will own the social work content for A1 under T1, and 427511 will coordinate the full document. Once we have leadership confirmation on the pilot scope in A7 and T9, we can close this thread and move on to drafting the joint protocol.

threads.thread_goal: Review and finalise the early identification and referral protocol and observation checklist.

messages.text: I have uploaded the first draft of the Early Identification and Referral Protocol as A2, based on the mapping in A1 and our agreed pilot scope in A7 and T9. This covers roles, steps, and consent requirements and is linked to T2. I have also added a proposal on how often we use the Classroom Observation Checklist (A3, T3). Could school colleagues review and comment on: 1) whether the steps are realistic in class, 2) any missing safeguarding or data protection points, 3) how often you think A3 can be used without overloading you?

Thanks for pulling A2 together. First impressions: the roles and steps are clear, and I like that you separated early concerns from urgent safeguarding. One question: in the classroom section, you suggest using A3 once per child every two weeks during the pilot. For some children that might be fine, but for others with more frequent changes we might need a lighter weekly note. Maybe we can define a minimum frequency in T3 and allow more frequent use when needed.

I agree that A2 reads clearly. On A3, I tested the draft checklist with one child this morning and it took about four minutes, which fits the T3 requirement. For frequency, I would suggest: baseline once when a child is first flagged, then a shorter follow-up version weekly for four weeks, then every two weeks if things are stable. We could build that into T3 and A3 so it is not too rigid but still structured.

From my side, the main concern is time during busy transitions. If we keep A3 to around five minutes as T3 says, I can manage a baseline and then shorter follow-ups. I like 511446's idea of a lighter weekly version. In A2, could we also make it clear that if we see a sudden serious change, we do not wait for the next scheduled checklist but act immediately and inform leadership?

I have a question on consent in A2. In the section about sharing information with social services, it says we obtain written consent from parents unless there is a safeguarding risk. Could we add a simple script or bullet points for how we explain this to parents, so that it is consistent with organisational guidelines and T11? That might also link later to the family engagement materials.

Good point. I can add a short consent explanation section to A2, aligned with our organisational guidelines under T11, and make sure it matches what we will later include in the family engagement script. For the checklist frequency, I like the idea of a baseline plus lighter weekly follow-ups. I will adjust T3 and A3 to reflect: baseline when a child is first flagged, then weekly short follow-ups for four weeks, then every two weeks if stable, with flexibility to act sooner if needed.

That frequency works for me. One more suggestion: in A3, could we group items into behaviour, learning, and safety, as T3 requires, and add a small space for notes on family context if parents share something relevant? That will help when we later look at patterns in the monitoring template.

Agree on grouping A3 items. I can help refine the wording so it is easy to complete quickly. For example, under behaviour we can list: withdrawal, aggression, clinginess, and under safety we can include unexplained marks or repeated accidents. I will add comments directly in A3 for T3.

Could we clarify in A2 who is responsible for starting A3? Sometimes I notice concerns first, but the teacher leads on communication with parents. Maybe A2 can say that any staff member can raise a concern and complete the first A3, but the teacher is responsible for making sure it is followed up and discussed with parents.

Yes, that is a good clarification. I will update A2 so that: any staff member can initiate a concern and complete the first A3, the class teacher coordinates follow-up and parent contact, and the social worker is involved once the concern meets the threshold described in the protocol. This should also help with consistency across classes, which is part of T11.

I have checked A2 against our school safeguarding and data protection procedures. It looks aligned: urgent risks still go through existing safeguarding routes, and the new steps focus on early support. I suggest we mark this version of A2 as the pilot version, with the understanding that we can tweak after the first few weeks if needed.

I support approving A2 for the pilot. The roles are clear, the consent section is helpful, and the link to A3 and classroom practice makes sense. For A3, with the updated structure and frequency you described, I am comfortable using it as our standard tool in the pilot.

Same here. I have added my final comments to A3 and they are minor wording tweaks. I think we can agree that A3, with baseline plus weekly short follow-ups for four weeks then every two weeks, is our final version for the pilot. We can document that usage pattern in T3 and in the training later.

Thanks all. I will now: 1) lock the current version of A2 as the pilot protocol under T2, 2) update A3 and T3 to reflect the agreed structure and frequency, and 3) note in T11 that A2 has been checked against school and organisational procedures. I will also flag that we may revisit A2 and A3 after we design the monitoring template so that indicators and fields line up.

threads.thread_goal: Define classroom support routines and align them with school procedures and workload.

messages.text: I have drafted a set of classroom support routines for identified at-risk children and added them into A4, linked to T6. There are eight strategies, such as predictable morning check-ins, calm corners, visual schedules, and small group support. Could you look at A4 and let me know: 1) which strategies feel realistic in your rooms, 2) anything that clashes with existing kindergarten procedures, 3) what would help us remember and share these routines (for example, a short guide or posters)? This will also connect to T10 and A8 for staff feedback during the pilot.

I like the structure in A4. The predictable morning check-in and visual schedules are already close to what we do, so those should be easy to standardise under T6. The calm corner is also helpful, but we need to be careful that it does not become a place where children are sent as a punishment. Maybe we can add guidance on how to introduce it positively.

From my room, the small group support and visual schedules are very workable. I am a bit unsure about the daily one-to-one check-in for every at-risk child, especially if we have several in one class. Maybe we can define a minimum, like a short check-in at arrival and one more during the day, and then we can add more if time allows.

Looking at A4 from a social work perspective, I think the routines are strong for emotional safety. Could we add a short note under each strategy about which social-emotional needs it supports, so that when we review cases we can link classroom routines to the concerns identified in A3? That would also help us explain to parents what we are doing.

From the community side, I like that A4 focuses on predictable routines and positive attention. To align with organisational guidelines and T11, we should check that none of the strategies conflict with behaviour policies or safety rules, for example around supervision in calm corners. I can do a quick check and add comments if I see any issues.

On the one-to-one check-ins, I agree we need to be realistic. How about we define in A4 and T6 that each at-risk child has at least one planned check-in per day, plus informal moments as possible, and we use the morning arrival as the priority time? That way we can still notice how they come in and adjust support.

Yes, that sounds like a good balance. I will update A4 so that: each at-risk child has at least one planned check-in per day, usually at arrival, and additional brief contacts when possible. I will also add the positive framing for the calm corner and link each strategy to the needs identified in A3, as 427511 suggested.

With that change, I feel more confident we can apply these routines even on busy days. Could we also include in A4 a short example of how to explain the calm corner to children, so they see it as a place to feel safe and calm, not as a time-out?

I have checked A4 against the behaviour policy and safety rules. Everything looks compatible as long as we keep children in sight and do not use the calm corner as a punishment. I will note this alignment in T11 so that leadership can see we have considered existing procedures.

On how we document and store these routines for staff access: I suggest we keep A4 as a short guideline in our shared drive and also create a one-page summary per class that lists which strategies are in use for each child. That summary could be stored with the monitoring template (A6) so that when we review progress we see both the concerns and the support in place.

I like the idea of a one-page summary per class. It will help new staff or substitutes quickly see what is in place. For T10 and A8, we could also add a simple question in the weekly feedback check-in about which routines are working well and which are hard to maintain, so we can adjust during the pilot.

Yes, a quick weekly question about routines would be helpful. Sometimes we realise a strategy is too complex only after trying it. If A8 and T10 capture that, we can simplify without waiting until the end of the pilot.

From the community side, storing the one-page class summaries alongside A6 will make it easier for us to understand what support is already in place when we review cases. We just need to ensure that any child-identifying information is handled according to data protection rules, which we can note in T8 and T12 when we finalise A6.

To bring this together: it sounds like we are comfortable including the eight strategies in A4, with the adjustments we discussed on check-ins and calm corners. I propose we confirm this set as the standard classroom support routines for the pilot under T6, and we document them in A4 plus the one-page class summaries stored with A6.

Agreed. The eight strategies in A4, with the clarified daily check-in and positive calm corner, feel both effective and realistic. Documenting them in A4 plus a class summary linked to A6 will make it easier to keep everyone aligned.

I will note in our records that the agreed set of classroom support strategies in A4 is now part of the pilot design under T6, and that documentation and storage will follow the shared drive guideline plus class summaries alongside A6. We can also reference this in A8 and T10 so that staff feedback explicitly covers how these routines are working.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on family engagement approach and home visit criteria.

messages.text: I have drafted the family engagement script and leaflet text as A5, linked to T4, and 361403 has added proposed criteria for home visits under T5. The script explains the Integrated Early Support Programme for At-Risk Children, how we use A2 and A3, and how we share information. The home visit criteria focus on repeated concerns, limited engagement, or unclear home situations. Could you review A5, T4, and T5 and comment on: 1) clarity and tone for parents, 2) whether the home visit criteria are realistic given limited visit times, 3) any safety rules we should add.

Thanks for pulling A5 together. From a community social work view, the tone is generally warm and clear. I suggest we simplify some phrases about consent and data sharing so they match the wording in A2 and our organisational guidelines. On T5, I have proposed that home visits are recommended when there are repeated concerns over four weeks, low response to school contact, or conflicting information about the child’s situation. We also need to state that visits are usually within core hours, with exceptions only for urgent safeguarding.

Reading A5, I think most parents will understand the leaflet. I like that it explains that the programme is about early support, not blaming. Could we add one short example, like how we might support a child who is very anxious at drop-off, so parents can picture it? On T5, the criteria sound reasonable, but we should be clear that sometimes a meeting at school might be a better first step than a home visit.

I agree with 499701. The script in A5 feels friendly, but a concrete example would help. Maybe we can also reassure parents that they can say if the timing of meetings or calls is difficult, and we will try to find options that work within our hours. For home visits in T5, I think it is important to say that they are voluntary unless there is a safeguarding concern.

From my experience, some parents feel nervous when they hear the word visit. In A5, could we explain clearly why we might suggest a home visit, for example to better understand routines or to see how we can support learning at home? That might reduce anxiety. On safety, I know social workers usually follow strict rules, so maybe we just need a short summary in T5 so school staff understand them too.

Yes, we can definitely explain the purpose more clearly. I will update T5 so that the criteria include: repeated concerns over four weeks, limited engagement despite school attempts, or unclear home routines affecting the child. I will also add a short section on safety procedures: visits planned in pairs when needed, logging visit details, and following organisational risk assessment. We will keep the wording simple in A5 so parents are not overwhelmed.

I will adjust A5 so that the consent and data sharing parts use the same simple wording as A2, and I will add one example about supporting an anxious child at drop-off, as 499701 suggested. I will also include a line that home visits are usually offered, not forced, unless there is a serious safety concern where social services must act.

Could we also add in A5 that parents can contact us if they have worries about their child, even if school has not raised anything yet? That might help with early engagement and reduce the risk of low family involvement.

Yes, and maybe we can mention that conversations can happen in person, by phone, or through a short written note, within our working hours. That flexibility might make it easier for parents who cannot come into school easily.

On the home visit criteria in T5, I want to check one point: we currently say visits are recommended after four weeks of repeated concerns. For some situations, that might be too long. I propose we add that if concerns are moderate but escalating quickly, we can consider a visit sooner after discussion between school leadership and social services, while still respecting workload and safety.

I agree we need that flexibility. I will adjust A5 so that when we talk to parents about possible home visits, we explain that timing depends on the situation and is agreed between school and social services. We will still keep most visits within core hours, as T5 states, but allow exceptions for urgent safeguarding following organisational rules.

With these changes, I feel comfortable using the script in A5 with parents. It feels respectful and clear. I think it will help when we first explain why we are using A3 and the new routines in A4 for their child.
Same here. Once you have updated A5 with the example and the extra lines on voluntary visits and contact options, I think we can approve it for the pilot under T4.

I have now updated T5 with: clear criteria for when a home visit is recommended, including repeated concerns, low engagement, unclear routines, and faster escalation when concerns grow quickly; standard steps for planning and documenting visits; constraints on visit times and safety procedures. From my side, these criteria and safety rules are ready to use in the pilot.

Great, I will finalise A5 now with the agreed wording and example, and mark it as the pilot version under T4. To summarise: we have a clear, parent-friendly script and leaflet, and agreed criteria and safety rules for home visits in T5 that fit within our time and safeguarding constraints.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in monitoring indicators, reporting template, and pilot start date.

messages.text: I have drafted the Monitoring and Reporting Template as A6, linked to T8, and proposed 3–5 indicators for child wellbeing and safety under T12. A6 includes sections for wellbeing, learning, and safety, plus fields for classroom routines from A4 and referrals under A2. I have also updated A7 with a tentative pilot start date based on our progress. Could you review A6, T8, and T12 and comment on: 1) whether the fields are clear and not too heavy, 2) if the indicators are meaningful and easy to track, 3) whether the proposed start date in A7 feels realistic given where we are with A2, A3, and A5?

Looking at A6, I like that the sections mirror A3 and A4. For each child, we record key wellbeing, learning, and safety notes plus which routines are in place. It might be helpful to limit the number of free-text fields so it does not become a long narrative. Maybe we can use simple scales for some indicators, like attendance and observed wellbeing, as T12 suggests.

I agree. For T12, the indicators you proposed (incidents, attendance, observed wellbeing, and engagement in class) make sense. Could we add a simple yes or no field for whether parents are engaged with the plan, based on A5 conversations? That might help us see if family engagement links to changes in wellbeing.

From a practical point of view, I think we can complete A6 weekly for each child if we keep it short. Maybe we can agree that we only update it once a week unless there is a serious incident, which we would log separately. That would keep T8 manageable.

On data protection, A6 looks fine as long as we store it in the secure system and limit access to relevant staff. Could we add a short note in T8 and T12 about where A6 is stored and who can see it, so that everyone is clear? That will also reassure parents if they ask.

Good suggestions. I will adjust A6 so that: 1) we use simple scales for attendance and observed wellbeing, 2) we keep one short free-text field per section for key notes, 3) we add a yes or no field for parent engagement linked to A5. I will also note in T8 that updates are weekly unless there is a serious incident.

On the indicators in T12, I think we can manage: 1) number of wellbeing or safety incidents, 2) attendance, 3) observed wellbeing score, 4) engagement in class, 5) parent engagement yes or no. That gives us a mix of quantitative and qualitative data without being too heavy.
Agree. We can also use A8 and T10 to collect quick staff feedback on whether A6 is workable in practice. If we find it is taking too long, we can simplify mid-pilot.

About the pilot start date in A7: if we finalise A2, A3, A4, and A5 this week, I think starting in two weeks gives us enough time to brief staff and talk to parents. Starting earlier might feel rushed, especially for explaining the programme to families.

I agree that two weeks from now is more realistic. We still need to run the short training session under T7, and staff will need time to read A2, A3, A4, A5, and A6. I suggest we set the pilot start date in A7 for two weeks from Monday, assuming we complete T2, T3, T4, T6, T8, and T12 by the end of next week.

That timeline works for me. I will update A7 with the proposed start date and list the readiness checklist: A2, A3, A4, A5, A6 finalised; T7 training delivered; and staff briefed on A8 and T10 for feedback. If there are no objections by tomorrow, we can confirm this as the pilot start date.

No objections from me. The two-week lead-in gives us time to plan classroom routines and talk to parents using A5. I will also start thinking about how to introduce A3 and A4 to colleagues in the training under T7.
Same here, I am comfortable with that start date. Once A6 is final, I can test it with a sample case as T8 requires, so we are not trying it for the first time on day one of the pilot.

On the protocol side, A2 is already approved for the pilot, and the changes we made for monitoring do not affect the core steps. I will just add a short note in A2 that some data will be recorded in A6 according to T8 and T12. That way we reconfirm that A2 remains our agreed protocol.

Thanks. To summarise: we have agreed on the indicators in T12, the structure and weekly use of A6 under T8, reconfirmed A2 as the protocol with a link to A6, and set a pilot start date in A7 for two weeks from Monday, subject to completing the remaining tasks. I will draft the training session under T7 to cover A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, and A8.
